messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajesh was 52 years old, a South Asian man living in the United States, divorced and working as a maid in a hotel housekeeping staff. He had always taken pride in being careful, quiet, and dependable, the kind of person who kept his head down and got through the work without making trouble. That self-understanding changed after a single day on the job, when a mistake he made ended in serious injury to another man. Rajesh did not describe the event as one long scene so much as a series of frozen pictures that returned to him with the force of a punch: the instant before he moved, the sudden chaos, and the sight of the man hurt in front of him. He said those moments were never remembered as a full story, only as sharp fragments, as if his mind had clipped the experience into separate images he could not hold together.

In the months that followed, he found that the memory could come back without warning. A sound in the hallway, the metallic rattle of a cart, or even a particular arrangement of cleaning supplies could drop him back into those few moments with no preparation. When that happened, it was not only fear that surged through him but intense rage, a hot and abrupt feeling that startled him as much as the memory itself. He would clench his jaw, feel his chest tighten, and become suddenly irritable in a way he struggled to explain to others. What disturbed him most was that the image would arrive so completely, as though the present moment had been swept aside and replaced by the exact same few seconds from that day. He became wary of anything in his surroundings that seemed even remotely similar to the setting of the incident, especially in the hotel corridors where he worked, because ordinary tasks could turn into an instant reminder.

Rajesh had worked in housekeeping for years, and after the injury he returned to the same building, but his relationship to the place changed. The corridors, carts, and service areas where he moved daily were no longer neutral parts of his routine; they were places where a memory could leap out at him without notice. He kept working because he needed the income, but he did so with a strained vigilance, moving through shifts with the sense that he had to stay on guard against his own mind. Some days he found himself staring at a cart or at the narrow stretch of carpet outside a guest room, seized by the old picture before he could stop it. He did not tell coworkers much. He had become more withdrawn and careful in conversation, especially because he felt ashamed that something in his own action had led to harm.

Over time, Rajesh’s explanation for the event hardened into self-blame. He was certain that the injury had happened because of the way he acted, and he returned to that belief often, turning it over in his mind as if there might be a version of events in which he had chosen differently and prevented everything. He spoke of having acted in ways that went against who he was, which mattered deeply to him because he had spent his adult life thinking of himself as responsible and respectful. The event felt to him like proof that he had violated his own values. That judgment colored how he saw his life afterward. He said that nothing felt meaningful anymore. The routines that had once given structure to his days now felt hollow, and even the effort of getting through work seemed detached from any larger purpose. He continued to perform his duties, but without the sense that the work connected to the person he believed himself to be.

His divorce had already left him living alone, and after the injury he became even more isolated in daily life. He went through the motions of work, then returned home to a quiet apartment where he was left with his thoughts and the recurring images. The combination of his own self-accusation and the way the memory could strike him suddenly made him feel as though he could not fully escape the event, no matter how many days passed. He had begun to fear not only the memory itself, but the possibility of encountering it at any time, in any place, with no warning. By the time he came for help, Rajesh was exhausted by the sense that the injury had split his life into before and after, and he was most afraid that the shame and meaninglessness would remain fixed forever. At the same time, he was hoping for some way to make sense of what happened without feeling permanently condemned by it.
